Death op a Favourite Charger þÿ On Tuesday last a favourite charger belonging to Col Love, the Commandant of the South Wales district, was obliged to be shot in consequence of its diseased and feeble state it was a beautilu! animal, thorough- bred, and of great power, and had carried its gallant owner throughout the campaign in Canada. Some time since it caught the thrush, which, from neglect on the part of the groom, turned to canker. Eventually it became tow weak to stand on its legs to be dtessed, and it was deemed advisable to put it out of its misery. Accordingly, on Tuesday, the poor animal was led into Dr Lawrence's garden where a grave had been dug for it, and where it was to meet its fate. A cloth having been tied over its face, Coi. Love fired, and it instantly fell dead. The feet were cut off and dissected by J Hughes, Esq., surgeon, and as a proof of the superior breed of the animal, it may be mentioned that the bone of t he leg was perfectly solid, like ivorv. and not at till carious; whilst (though t tie horse was not a large one), the size of the leg bone was that ol a carl tiorse. þÿ Welshman.

An Evening at Delhi þÿ þÿ The evening is the best time for getting an insight into tiie ways and manners of the people ; 1 therefore gladly accepted the otier ol Captain Bowen to ride with him on his elephant thmugli the Streets of Delhi, his sutwar, mounted on a camel, trotting on before to make way for us. We proceeded to the silver market, the broad street which intersects Delhi from east to west. When we turned into it, at the extreme west end, the most interesting scene of Indian common life met our eyes. The houses in this street are of two and three stoiics, built of sandstone and brick On the ground floor are the open bazaars, from w hich innumctablr lamps diffused a light, equal to that of the finest illumination : the upper sto lies are the residence of the merchants, where at the open windows, or in the balconies or verandahs, the women and girls, gailv dressi-d, were gazing upon the multitude below. The people passed in crowds from shop to shop, elephants and camels endeavmed carefully to make their way through this living mass ; here were the merchants praising their goods, there were handsome female figures, in their airy white garments, giving vent to their joy in laughing and jesting: bands of music were playing, while female dancers and buffoons collected a little circle around them, who expressed their admiration more by gestures than bv words, A cunning fiuit seller offered his hookah to every passer by, to entice customers. Jewellers now and then opened their caskets and displayed their beautiful

ornaments of gold, silver, precious stones, and pearls ; tor the work of I fie goldsmiths of Delhi, especially in filigree, are more ingenious. tasteful, and inexpensive than anywhere in India, and far excel those of Genoa. Paintings on ivory, portraits, as well ns buildings and processions, tire executed here in the greatest perfection, and would do honour even to our best artists. Not metcly is the

-. þÿ - þÿ likeness admirable, but the delicacy and fidelity of the execution are very great. Wn rode about for a couple of hours through this busy world, and it was late in the evening before we reached the þÿcamp. þÿ Tiavets in India. A Valuable þÿCargo. A - vessel which has recently arrived in the London Docks had on board the most valuable cargo, and the greatest quantity of spirits, ever recollected to have been imported in one vessel, consisting of no less than 2000 casks and 3000 cases of brandy, tiie duty on which alone, if paid, would amount to the sum of neatly 60,000/. The importation in this instance, however, being from America, and, eonse qnently. inadmissible for home use, under the navigation laws, the whole of this valuable cargo has been necessarily entered for exportation only. Financial Scheme þÿ The great art of taxation is to get as much as you can, and to levy duties on those niticles which are likely to be the most productive. Now, the stamp on receipts is ail well enough, but a stamp on bills would tie much better, for it has been ascertained that receipts are rare in proportion to bills, for there are at the In vest compulation at least two thousand of the latter to one of the former. Ii it were compulsory on every tradesman to send in his bill upon a stamp, a much larger revenue would be collected than can he obtained tind 'r the present system. Eet anyone look through his own private papers, and he will find the preponderance of bills over receipts to be very considerable, and when it is remembered how very large a class are never in ilie habit of seeitur a receipt at all. it seems a piece of gross partiality to let the burden fall oti the paying part of the public, while the dishonest mall who never settles an account, and never, therefore, gives occasion for a receipt, contributes nothing to the public income. Society in general would also benefit by the proposed change, for tradesmen would not be so pertinacious in Sending in their accounts where there is no chance of getting the money, if a proper reduction in the shape of a stamp were to be put upon the very obnoxious practice. -Punch.

From the " N., V. Journal of Commerce.' THE OREGON QUESTION. We publish below, a W ashinglon letter which we (ind in the Richmond Enquirer, and n extract from the Chraleslon Mercury, relating to the Oregon question, and the declarations of the Biitish Ministers, la regard to the latter we can onlv say that we hope and believe it does not speak the sentiments of the Administration. The remarks of the Charleston editor are in the main appropriate. But we presume there is no idea of calling an Extra Session. Certainly there is no reason for it. according to any ideas which we possess, of the nature of the present crisis. The remarks of the British Ministers were made under the impression, or at least under an apprehension that President Polk designed to take the Oregon question out of the hands of the negotiators, and reler its solution to the power of the strongest. Such being the case, their remarks were as pacific as could possibly have been expected ; and indeed much more so. After having asserted her claim for so many years, and professed to believe it well founded, England could not. with any show of honor, suffer that claim to be trampled under foot. The last two sessions of Congress have abounded with bulking speeches, offensive to England, and disgraceful to the United States. But the British Ministry could not well take cogniza ce of them. The Inaugural of President Polk gave them an opportunity to say what they had long desired to say. viz that thev had rights in the Oregon territory us well as we; and that those rights must he regularly

extinguished, before we could come into exclusive possession. For our own part, we are glad England has shown her hand. We shall now act with our eyes open If we choose to insist upon every square mile of Oregon, rather than submit the matter to arbitrators or compromise, we can do so, but þÿ , If on the other hawi, we are prepared to grant as well as ask concessions of extreme claims, or to refer the case to disinterested parties, all will be well. Correspondence of the Richmond Enquirer. Washington Acrii. 25. Ever since the arrival of the Caledonia, our city has been filled with the conjectures and rumours in relation to the deliberations of the Cabinet upon the important despatches which she brought, the debate in Parliament, and the tone of the British press upon the Oregon question. One thing is certain þÿ the President is determined to maintain our national rights at every hazard, let come what mav. Ureal Britain may depend upon this; and, if she is determined to pursue the course pointed out by Sir Robert Peel, we may at once prepare for the issue ; and every American heart will utter but one sentiment upon the subject. Oregon is ours, and we will defend it at the hazard of the die, a), though Great Britain may bluster and brag about her forbearance as much as she pleases. In (lie ncgoo.iunon between Mr. lluskisson and Mr. Gallatin. she never, for one moment, asserted, that, she had a right to that teiritorv ; hut, on the contrary, admitted ours up to the 49ih degree. When I.ord Ashburton

came tt) the U. States as a special ambassador it was the prevailing opinion, that he was authorized to settle all differences, but. in this opinion, we were mistaken þÿ and it is rather late in the dm tor the British Ministry to as

«gnrtMTn gcrt theit right 10 this territory, unless they i are prepared for war; for such will be the evident tendency of things. The President, in his Inaugural Address, has boldly and beautifully declared the sentiments of the American people upon this momentous question, front which he cannot and will not tie part without surrendering the national honor, a thing impossible for one, whose heart and soul are filled with love for the glory and character of his country. The British Ministry do not understand the true character of our people, and the Government under which we live. They think that here, as there, the Government is independent of the people; hut in this they deceive themselves; for the humblest citizen is fully conscious of his identity with the Government, and when her honor and rights are invaded, so are his. This is the beauty of our Government, and the people feel an interest in defending her honor; but in England where the law of piimogeniture prevails which entails upon the people a landed aristocracy who have been eating out the very vitals of the productive classes lor two centuries, the people feel no such respon. sibilitv and are eager for some great revolution to lake place, that they may assert and maintain their rights. 1 fie British Ministry «enm to flatter themselves at the idea that our slave population is an incumbrance, that it will require our whole lorce to keep them in their places but in this they reckon without their host, for our old men, who are muster-

free can attend to our domestic concerns, wlrie the young men can go foith to battle, bearing the stars and stripes of their country. A war with England would unite us as a people ; but. with her, it would be the element ot her national downfall. Her people ate ttneasv þÿ they know they are wronged and impoverished by a heartless ar.stocraey, and that, bv perpetuating her nationality, and extending her dominion over the whole world, thev would be rivetting the chains of oppression upon themselves and their posterity. þÿ of the Now. in a state of profound peace, she is compelled to keep a large standing army at home, to keep down die people ; yet she has the hardihood to talk about war with the Young Giant," who came out two wars victorious when she was not half as strong as she is at. present. What! a war with the United States ! In such an event, what would she Jo with the bold dissatisfied spirits of Manchester, Birmingham and Sheffield, where she is compelled to keep a strong force, and particularly when the manufacturing establishments ate idle, and ike people out of employment? What will she do with five million of dissatisfied Irishmen, who have been groaning under British tyranny (over since their unholy union with England? What avill she do with her Canadian and her East India possessions? These are pertinent ques» tions and she had better look well at coming evenls before she is swa. lowed op bv those from whom she expects support. The British people love the beautilui isle ot their nativity,

but they despise their cruel rulers who tax them to death to support a heartless aristocracv, nnd a host of German f'rinces. We tell Sir Koliert Peel, with an American heart, that we ate ready to riefend our rights and our honor, no matter from what quarter tliev are invaded: and when the war bugle shall sound, thousands of swords will leap from their scabbards in defence of liberty and ry iftlity. t'rom Bell's Weekly Messenger, London, April þÿ 28, 1815. DREADFUL CASE OF RELIGIOUS FANATICISM. In a loiter from Cairn, dated April (>, we find the following dreadful illustration of the sanguinary deeds which are sometimes perpetrated under the influence of religious fanaticism when it developes itself in the form of revenge : þÿ þÿ One of those laoaticai outrages which from time to time unhappily occur in Turkey and Egypt, has recently taken place at Damiettea and has caused much indignation among our diplomatic agents and the Christian population in general. A Christian Copt and a Mussulman Arab having quarreled, in the heat of argument mutually abused each other ; the Arab heaped upon the Copt, his relatives, and his sect, every available invective and anathema, which the Copt retorted by making free with the Prophet and his descendants. The enraged Arab immediately reported the matter to the Cadi, who, opening his code of laws, found it therein laid down that every blasphemer of the Prophet should sutler death. I he Copt was instantly arrested, and as a preliminary measure, without the slightest investigation, was bastinadoed bv the infliction ol 500 blows upon the soles of his feet, and then thrown into prison, On the following day he was dragged before Ah Bey, the governor in Council, by Whom he was condemned to be burnt ulioe ! This sentence was, however, subsequently changed, it being feared that the Giand Pacha would not approve ol it, as it is well known, not only to Musstilmen but also to Europeans, that his Highness Mehemct

Ali, very much to his honour, is one of the most tolerant of his faith. The punishment of this poor old Copt, 75 years of age, was therefore changed, he was again most unmercifully bastinadoed, receiving 1000 blows up on his feel and body, in this stale was paraded through the streets of Damieita on a hullulo, with his face to the tail, a cr..ss fixed at his back, dogs and Cats tied round his neck, and pelted and tormented by the populace, who kept him an the buffalo bv ropes tied round his body, and which they held in their hands. His face and his body were, moreover, daubed over with warm pitch by some boatmen who were repairing a boat in the neighbourhood. I need hardly add, the poor victim of this fiendish persecution died shortly afterwards No doubt ample satisfaction, will he demanded by the consular representatives from the Viceroy, who Still remains in this citv : but, as yet, what his highness has done is scarcely considered satisfactory enough, viz., the degradation of Ali Bey, the governor, his committal lo the Castle of Aboukir, the exile of the Grand C fie i k of Damieita, and condemning tiie governor lo pay an indemnity to the family of the martyred Copt. However, if these orders are rigidly carried out, and if it is true that the offending governor has also been sentenced to six þÿyears impi isonment, as it is said, then it would be dittocult to say what more could be expected of the Viceroy. His highness Itas at all times a most difficult, arduous, and trying part to
perform, and at his advanced age it is almost wonderful that be gets through the cares and difficulties of the government as he dues.

We find in the New Bedford Mercury (American paper) a long and minute account ol a mutiny which occurred on board the whaling stiip Sharon, in November, 1842, and of the manner in which the ship was retaken from the mutineers by a single person, Mr. Clough, the third mute. The Sharon, after a ciuise near the Caroline Islands, had procured supplies at Ascension, and was preparing for the voyage, when 11 of her crew deserted, and were not tetaken. She shipped a new crew of 17, including six natives of the Islands. On Sunday, November 6, in latitude 2 deg. 20 sec. notth, long. 162 east, both boats were lowered in chase of whales ; Captain Norris, a þÿI onuguese boy who acted as steward, and three ol the natives being left on boaid. The boats soon captured a whale, which lire ship took alongside, and the boats went in pursuit ol another. At three o'clock p nn the boat ol Mr. Smith, the mate, being about a mile and a halt from the ship, perceived a signal flying and pulled towards tier. On coming wuhiu hailing distance, they were told by the hoy, wbo was aloft, that the natives fuid killed Captain Non is, and weie in possession of the ship. Just then, one of ttie natives, entiiely naked, leaped upon the taflVuil, and, brandishing a spear, dated the crew to come on boaid An aimed native siood guard at each side, and hammers, belay ing pins, and other missiles had been collected lor their use, and wrie hurled furiousiy at the bunt, though without much injury. The male then wailed tor the

oihcr boat, and consulted as lo the best method ot retaking the ship. It was purposed that tiie boats should advance and board her, one upon each side, at the same time ; but Mr. Smith, the mate, who had become master by the þÿcaptain s death, proposed that both crews should make the attack with one boat, and leave him in the other, '1 his proposal was received with no favour, the men declaring they would sooner start lor the nearest laud and risk the chance of escape. Mr. Clough, who had acted as Mr. Smith's steersman, had several times darted his lance at the savage on the talliail ; hut the distance was too great, and he requested to he rowed nearer ( hut Mr Sm th thought the danger too great, and refused to approach the ship. All . Clough proposed several other devices, but, in default of aid from others, resolved to retake the ship himself. He accordingly, after dark, was taken by the boat ahead of the ship at some distance, to avoid exciting suspicion, and taking a knife in his teeth to defend himsell from sharks, which had been attracted by the whale, swam to the ship, after a hard struggle of an hour and a half, dm mg which two sharks kept him company, tiut uid not oiler to molest him. Having reached the ship he dived under, seized the rudder at the heel, and climbed to the starboard cabin window, through which he made his entry. Laying aside his clothes, and ascertaining that no suspicion existed ol his being on board, he groped about fur arms, and lound two cutlasses and two muskets,

which he loaded. While loading one lie heard some one descending the stairs. Kun mug thither he giasped a cutlass, and a struggle ensued. \lr Clough succeeded in thrown g his antagonist, thrust out one of his eyes, and left him for dead, having been severely wounded himself in the contest. No sooner had lie Ich Ins supposed rtciini, than he got

up and furiously renewed 'he attack, but finally fell down from loss of Idood. Alt. Clough, going attain lo the gangway, saw another person with a cutting spade: he shot him from below, through tiie heart, but just as he fired the spade was thrown at him, and disabled his left arui. A thin person can.e to the gangw ay, with another spade, but soon went lot ward. Air. Clough then hailed the boats, which were very near told them he had killed two of the mutineets, and was himself dangerously wounded, and urged them to come at once on board. 1 hey refused, as thev had heard but one discharge, feared only one had been killed, and they did not think it sate Alter about half an hour, hearing no noise, they came abuaid stiuck alight, and went mlo the cabin The man with whom Air. Clough had fiisl contended was lound on the transom, his body covered with gore. He did not move, but merely groaned, whereupon Air. Smith, the mate, fiied a musket at him, and he was thrown into the sea. The deck was tracked with doited blood ; the headless bodv of Captain Norris was found, with that ol one of his tnuiderers. The other mulineer jumped overboard, but returned, surrendered, and was taken to Sydney. I he Shaion completed her voyage under Mr. Smith, Mr. Clough acting as second male. DUTCH EMBASSY TO JAPAN. The ISieuwe Hotterdutnsche Com ant pubfishes some inieresnng detuils respecting the mission /.I the Dutch Embassy Exiruordina ry to the empire of Japan, which may he thus summed up. The ship of the line in which the embassy arrived at Decima, the only port where the one annual merchant ship of the Dutch was allowed to tiade was received with extraordinary honours by the Japanese autlior ities. The usual offensive preliminary of unshipping the guns, ammu. nition, and tiller of the vessel, and keeping them on shoie Under government charge, was dispensed with on this occasion. The officers of the vessel also, contrary to custom, and for the first time were allowed to retain their arms on going oa shore. The letter addressed by the King of Holland to the Emperor Japan was received with the of greatest veneration, and despatched to Jed do (the capital) with an immense escort of people, the train of which is indeed two leagues in extent ; because the government w as desirous that this letter should be read in presence of all the princes and dignitaries of the empire. By an express order of the Emperor it was commanded that the escort should avoid the passage of large rivers, so as to avoid anv casunlity. The answer of the Emperor was not expected Until the commencement of the present vear. It wits confidently believed by the Dutch that more favourable terms of commercial intercom se þÿ would he conceded to the mission by their ancient and faithful þÿally. as the Emperor
is st\ led. which would lead to a great exter. sion of Commerce; and other nations it is

curiously remarked, wilt have to thank the Dutch for having by prudent means, opened that empite to civilization and put an cod to the system of Monopoly and insolation so long existing With regard to Japan. The well known fact is, that the Dutch themselves have been the authors of this exclusive dog in the manger system, being content with a partial and degrading exception themselves, so long as they could keep other nations out altogether. We should not, perhaps be wide of the mark, Were we to say that it is the report of British cannon in China which is opening Japan to me Dutch : and it is to be hoped that our government will not lie slow in taking measures lor securing for England a share in the extended trade with Europe, which must, before Jong follow the preseut effet ts of the Dutch.

The following a.e the leading features of the scheme : Three provincial colleges are to be established : one in Cork, for the south of Ireland; one in l.imeiick, or Galwav, tor the west ; and one in Derry, or Beltast, tor the north. For certain reasons, explained by Sir J. Giaham, the probability is that Hellast will be the favoured spot lor the north. The sum wanted lor the erection of the three colleges is estimated at about 100.000/-, and the annual charge for the endowment of each college will be 0000/. Each college to have a principal, with a salary of 10U0/- a year, and about ten or twelve piofessors, vviih a salaiy ot Mill, n year each. The professors to be nominated by the Crown, and to be removable lor sufficient cause; the principals to have a residence within the walls of the colleges, but the professors and the students to dwell without. HAY I I. President Guerrier is said to have died under singular circumstances, which do great credit to his humanity. The ten persons lately reported hy a contemporary to have been shot, were not executed, but the order for death was laid before him for his signature. This, however, he refused to affix to it, as he did not consider that they deserved death ; 'and,' he is reported to have said, ' I am an old man, myself, and have but a few short days to live ; why, therefore, should I deprive mv fellow creatures of life,?' Having said this he fell hack and expired!

The American Barque Josephine from New Yo'k. arrived yesterday, and brought us tiles to the 20th May; .after a careful perusal, we cannot find any definite of decided movement on the part of the United Stales government with reference to the grave question now pending between it and the government of Great Britain. The transatlantic Press with very few exceptions is rabidly belligerant, hut newspaper wars and rumours of war are scarcely worthv of notice, except that they denote clearly the tone and temper of public opinion, of which they are the bond slaves in the majority of instances, and raiely lead it, since their interest impels them nolens volens to swim with the stream. The Weekly Herald which boasts of the laigest circulation in the States of any journal, breathes defiance to Britain in almost every leader. According to that print, Mr J. C. Calhoun is to proceed to England on a special mission armed with extraordinary powers to cover both the set tlement of the Oregon question, and to negotiate a commercial treaty of a character to draw closer than ever the ties of friendship between the United Slates and Great Btilain, and it adds with the most hare faced coolness; þÿ If a broad and comprehensive cummer cial treaty, favourable and equitable to the agriculture, commerce, and manufactures of both nations can be carried out, we do not believe that any difficulty will grow out of the claims of the British Government to a small portion of the Oregon Territory. II the British Government listen with cordiality to

such a plan of negotiation, and carry it out to the fullest extent, the peace of the two countries may be preserved for many yeats to come, and happiness wilt prevade both nations! the result of the new condition of things. But we are persuaded that no other alternative will succeed. It this mode of adjusting the difficulties between England and the United Slates should fail, then there must inevitably he an appeal to physical force, and that at no distant day. Clever and knowing as the above scheme Vnay be, if any attempt be made to lay it he fore the British Government, we are confident it will t>o beyond the art of Mr, Calhoun or any oth.-r American Diplomatist to draw the wool over its eves so easily as they seem to imagine they can. Moreover we do not think that the American government will select Mr Calhoun if they even contemplate attempting by negotiation to adjust the conflicting claims amicably, such a selection would he a deliberate insult to the British government, and the inlerencc that all cool and rational men Would draw, would he that America com ts hostilities and in order to bring a rupture about selects the most offensive agent in her dominions and sends him with an olive branch in one hand, and a war manifesto in the other The Herald winds up its diatribes by staling that no danger can arise to America from any threatening attitude of England. That power may send as many fleets and armies to Oregon, and Canada as it can, but fifty nr n hundred thousand men collected on the

Canadian frontier from all parts of the Union, would soon settle the Oregon and Canadian, or any other question on this continent, in such a wav that all the p >Wnr of Gieat Bti tain could nut prevent or invalidate.

The extracts which we insert in our columns this day from (he latest Atnerieau papers ip. the island confirm in every particular the news we announced to our leaders some Weeks past, ot a treaty having been entered into between Mexico and Texas, recognising the independence of the latter republic On condition ot her non annexation to the United State. It is also asserted on authority, said, to be relied on, that England certainly and France probably has endorsed the treaty and thus guaranteed the independence of Texas. Vague (lints ate thrown out by some <d the Journals that it is bv no means unlikely that a collision may take place between the British and American squadrons at present in the Gulf iu consequence of the Government of the U. S deeming it an obligation on their part to protect the territory of Texas from the interference of a third power pending the decision of the question of annexation, nor is this supposition so unreasonable as at first view might he imagined. When France and England acknowledged the Texan Requblic and admitted it into the vast community of nations, they undertook to procure at a fitting time (he recognition of the same from Mexico, t. e. when it became Certain that Mexico was unable to resuhjugate the revolted province by force of arms, or in other wards when the Texan had proved to the world they were able to maintain their own independence, and were do facto a nation. That acknowledgement that they have now wrung from Mexico,

tardilv it is too true, and to serve their own ends hut still prior to the expiration of the period fixed on by both powers. It is not imuossibie that Mr. Folk and Ins partv mav claim Texas, as American territory, stranger things have come to pass. þÿ lhe late President Was of that opinion and Mr. Calhoun sanctioned the assumption, and it is evident as the sun of noon day that frontier lines are fallacies when they wisli to graspt or according to the pet. diplomatic phrase ot American statesmen annex any portion ot the continent. The relations between the States and England are becoming graver daily, the mouldering embers are smoking fitlully, a very little breath will fan ihem into a flame, a very trifling untoward affair may let slip the dogs of war, and both the old and new continents may he trodden by hostile armies. Even in the þÿMc Leod aflair the two countries were not committed to the extent they are at present, bitter angry feelings are rife between the masses of both countries, all the intelligence and wealth on either side is for peace, because the best interests of both nations are interwoven with it, but the questions at issue are agitating the public mind toils inmost þÿrecesses one gun fired, aye ! even accidentally, and there can he no retreating þÿ and the broad Atlantic in all pioba hi 1 1 tv will he the first battle ground. We anxiously await further news tor the obscurity of these absorbing questions becomes daily more dim and puzzling.

IMPORTANT FROM MEXICO. The Washington Union contains advices from Vera Cru to the I Oth May brought to Pensacola bv the U. S. brig Somers, specially despatched by Commodore Connor, of the U. S Squadron oil Vera Crux. They are as follows : From the Union. The News op the Day. The most interesting news of the present dav is the accounts we are receiving from Mexico and Texas. First we have an arrival at New Orleans from Havana, with the circuitous intelligence which it brings front Vera Cruz; and then, still later and more direct accounts, received thence through the mysterious arrival of the Relampago, wnh her single passenger, and her undt fined purposes, and chartered for the trip at an expense of $f,000. from Vera Craz, to New Oilcans. These accounts followed each other with a rapidity and with a mystery Which aie cal culated to give rise to considerable interest and busy speculations. Is it true it is asked, that the Relampago does bring the declaration of war from Mexico against the United States? Is it true that she brings positive intelligence of the signing of a treaty by Me ioo, which recognises the independence of Texas? It happens to be within our power to give the most direct solution, from the most authentic materials, received in this city of these two problems i Mexico has adopted a trealv of independence ; and therefore she pretends to or bear the declaration ol war against the United States. We publish copious details from the letters which are before us, as they were received by the brig Somers despatched by Capt. Connor,

at Pensacola, as late as the 1 Oth of M a v from Vera Cruz. Wo have also received authentic letters from New Orleans, which discredit the report of war, as brought bv the Relampago, and ascribe her arrival either to stock jobbing schemes, or some commercial speculations.

Eiom Dell's Weekly Messenger, London April 7, 1845. INDIA AND CHINA. Through the activity of our indefatigable dailv contemporaries, the Times md the Morning Herald, we are put in possession ot intelligence irotn India and I bins, io anticipation of the overland mail from Bombay. Of the preparations tor a war in the I unjaub there was little doubt, tor troops, arms, and ammunition ot all kinds were hastening to the frontiers. The general opinion was, that the chances ot an invasion ot that country were not great until after the next monsoon, that is, in September next ; hut these events ntav be hastened by an application on the part of the boy king Dhuleep, or ot his mother Ghundee, who are likely within a short time to be compelled by the unrestrained and overbearing licentiousness of the soldiery to seek for the protection of the British power. Ghoolab Singh had already raised the standard of revolt, and was prepared to defend himself in the mountainous districts "t Jumboo. Some of the Sikh troops had proceeded to a'taclt him in his fastnessses. There appears to he a great wisli on the part of the British troops to measure swords with the Sikhs. It was rumoured that Sir Henry Hardinge was preparing to proceed next summer into the north-west provinces, but that the army against the I'onjaub would tie commanded bv Sir Hugh Cough. IJIiost Mahommed and his son Akhbur Ki.an are engaged iu watching the proceedings in the Punjaub, with the evident intent of pouncing upon Peshawur at a favourable opportunity. Aklihar Khan was at

Jelliilahad. and trying to win over to ins cause the heads of the Kin bar clans, in order to insure him a sate passage tor his troops to the Sikh frontiers. The disturbances in the southern Mahratta country had been put down. Those of the S.iwunt Warree country have also ceased. The rebels have been lorced out ol the jungles, and compelled to seek refuge in the Goa territory, where, although not surrendered, they have been disarmed, and measures taken to prevent their again presuming to produce confusion in the disiricts subject to British rule. The government of Bombay sent two dillerent missions on the subject to (tie Portuguese Governor ot Goa, who, by his conduct in sheltering the rebels, has become responsible lor their future acts. Golonel Outram has been appointed in the room of Golonel Ovaus, who has retired to Europe.

Aoen. þÿ A letter from Aden, daicd March 11, contains the following passage: þÿ The Arabs have not yet attacked Aden, but accounts continue to he received from lite interior that they are still assembled in large bodies from their having deferred their march on Aden so long it may be considered a strong sign that but little unanimity exists either tu their councils or operations. The garrison at present in Adeu is fully capable of repelling any attpek, however well planned or bravely led. There are now 1200 European and 1000 native troops in the place besides her Majesty's sloop Serpent, the Hon Company's sloop Elphinstone and brig Euphrates shortly to be reinforced by her Majesty's frigate Fox, another sloop and schooner. besides a steam frigate to be permanently placed on the station. All the troops, European and native, continue healthy Supplies from the interior are abundant. The inhabitants of the towns near Aden are beginning to turn their attention to the cultivation of European vegetables, for which the soil is verv favourable. Indeed, growing vege aties for the Aden market they find a lucrative occupation, as they are at all times certain of a good remuneration and ready sale. It is to be regretted that advantage is not taken of this growing spirit of inquiry, which seems to have been suddenly exceed in their minds, to introduce an improved system of horticulture and agriculture."

Discovery op a Murder by a Dog þÿ In the month of August last year, a regiment of the Queen's was quartered at Valencia, and a detachment was billeted at a small village near, named Ilos.ifa ; ihe officer commanding it, Don Rafael" Marquis de Turin, was lodged at a farmer's 1'edro lor t i, the besi hot.se in the village. C Fedro had a wife, Vieenta f young and extremely handsome, to whom be was passionately attached. Lb foiethe arrival of the troops in the village she had been loud of her husband, tranquil, and devout J but after the Maiquis had been a short tune in their house, Fedro peiceived an alteration in his wife's manners, fits of foolish gaiety were succeeded by profound melancholy ; in the presence of Don Rafael she was much agitated, and in his absence impatient for his return. Fedro's suspicions were aroused j he watched the pair, and soon had convincing proof of his dishonour. He, however, concealed his knowledge of their guilt, awaiting a favourable opportunity for vengeance 5 and matters thus went on lor a short time, when suddenly Don Rafael disappeared. It was at lirsi thought his duties had called him back to Madrid, but a considerable time elapsing without his return, suspicion was a w akened. A peasant recollected having one night, about the period of the disappearance ol the Marquis, heard a single hut terrible cry þÿ a cry of agony. Fedro repelled all charges w ith hi illness, and lor want of proofs t he matter diopped. The period of the grand chase ol tochas

(a sort of bird) arrived, and men, horses and dogs assembled on the hanks of the river þÿ Among the dogs was one formerly belonging to the Marquis, and which, on arriving at one part of the river, became greatlv agitated, pliniced in. and brought out a human band. þÿ Running straight to Rosafa, he placed his burden on the threshold of the door of Fedro Ferrer. His wife immediately fainted, and Fedro, struck bv remorse, avowed his having murdered Don Ralael one night, out his body into pieces, and thrown them into dillerenl parts of the river, thinking ihus to elude detection. From the St Thomas Times, May 24, 1815 We insert in this day's number various extracts trotn very late American Journals brought by the brig Cordelia which art i ved jesierday from New York þÿ and it would appear from them that the public mind is much oivided regarding the declaration of the British Ministry concerning the Oregon question þÿ it docs not appear at ail likely to us that the President will call an exira ses sion of Congress as I lie declaration does not render any immediate action imperative, or called lor, on the part of the executive of the United States. One thing we aie muili pleased to notice þÿ that the American press Willi very few exceptions admit the tone of language used by the British Ministers to have been calm and dignified, but do not attempt to disguise the gravity of ihe crisis þÿ we must confess we cannot see, how the point at issue can be amicably adjusted þÿ the popular voice undoubtedly is strongly in favour of the immediate seizure, and occupation of the whole region in dispute, and it is not probable that Great Britain will tamely permit the districts which have been so long in the actual occupation of incorporated companies of her subjects (and when she has erect ed several military stations) to be wrested from her without a struggle þÿ or that she will be content merely to enter her protest against the act. Nor is the prize unworthy of being contended for by two great nations. It may become at no very distant period a high road to the Pacific þÿ connected by steam to China. The sea beard to a maritime nation

is of incalculable value þÿ and although litile be at present known of the extent of iis natural resources and capabilities, the enterprize of the colonists will rapidly develope them. But, we cannot Dulliciently deplore the short Sighledness of the policy which would risk a sanguinary war and the horrois which must inevitably follow in its train, lor the sake of acquiring the disputed territory without iurilici delay, whetn lime and the

onward roll of the tide of emigration fr«in the States would settle the question without any appeal to arms being requisite. England has so many outlets for bet surplus population which can be reached in much le»s time and at far less ex pence than Oregon, that voluntary emigration thither is not likely to become a mania among her subjects whilst the American population most in a very few years it left to their own fate out number the inhabitants of Euiopeati biith, and be enabled by commanding the majority of votes to apply for, and gain admission into the Union.

An Argument for an Execution þÿ A case was tried a tew days since before the Superior Court of Connecticut, which exinbi ted some singular features, and pics- riled one of the very lew instances in which the prisoner himself comes befote a couit of justice with an argument in favour of capital punishment. and finds his plea overru d bv the court. One Bennett, a convict in tne sta e prison, was on trial for an attempt t< murder Mr. Norton, one of the overseers. Bennett refused the assistance of counsel, and made a formal address to the court in his own behalf ; insisting with great earnestness upon being sentenced to deaih. He had murder in his liean, he said, and he ought to be hanged It was folly to fri'ter down the crime to any 'ess heinous offence, and he quoted Scripture to prove the impiopriety of Jetliighim oil with mitigated punishment. He bad lately " got religion," and was satisfied that his conversion this time was substantia! «ed to be depended on 5 some of his burner "exercises" in that way having turn- d out shams, he had taken pains this time to make sure on that point. It was therefore matter of moment to him that he should be put out of the way of a reiapse into misi hief again. The court had a difleient view of the law from that of the prisoner, and, instead of ordering him to be banned, simply sentenced him to lour years' confinement in the State Prison. His head presents a puzzle fur phrenologists, being very defective in the organ of combotiveness and in the organs

It appears that a larger crop of sugar is expected in all the islands than has been obtained for many years. Jamaica, it is said, will make 50 000 hhds , Demerara 45 000, and the other islands one third to a half more than usual þÿ Agricultural improvements are paid considerale attention to, and the plough and other implements of husbandry are fust coining into use, beneficially replacing manual labour, and no doubt will in the end enable the West India planter to compete with slave grown sugar. Lord Elgin, the Governor of Jamaica, laid the foundationstone of the new Penitentiary on the 22d of February. 'l'his was, perhaps, no more than could be reasonable expected from such a large body of men, totally uneducated, cast loose upon society try their emancipation in mass, but will doubtless be gradually corrected by suitable laws and public institutions lor their general instruction

THE HI V F.Il PLATE. Accounts have been received from Hoenos Avres to the lfith of January. The intelligence is of considerable importance to British commerce, and shows the necessity ol rendering the proposed intervention as prompt as possible. The Buenos Avrean government lias declared a total blockade of the port of Monte Video against the ships of all nations, in the place 'of the partial blockade which has existed lor some time as relates to vessels carrying provisions and munitions of war. Nothing, therefore, is now left lor the English, French, and Brazilian governments but t» decide whether they will allow the commerce of their respective countries to lie altogether shut out from the north hank of the lliver Plate, or will put an end to this ruinous struggle at once. What renders this decision the more necessary i», that the Buenos Ay roan government has issued another decree forbidding all Communication with Corrlentrs, Paraguay, and, in fact, witli the whole interior of South America, until what is called "I- gal order" (that is, the tyranny of llosas) is reestablished in Gorrienles. It appears that the public income of Buenos Avres for the present year is rather more than 40,000 000 of paper dollars, whilst the expenditure is estimated at upwards of 50.000,000, leaving a deficiency'of 10.000.000. In the hope of raising increased supplies a decree Was issued on the 20th of December, imposing the following duties, which fall almost entirely on foreign commerce, namely: þÿ

Three dollars per ton on national vessels trading to foreign parts. Of these vessels there are scarcely any, so that the tax is a sham so tar as they tire concerned. Four dollars per ton on the vessels of foreign countries riot having reciprocity treaties with Buenos \ vres, and three dollars per ton on the vessels of foreign countries having such treaties. On the l()th January, there were 112 foreign vessels in the port of Buenos Avres. of rather more, on the average, than 200 tons each, the tax on which would

Nor is this all. for, besides lliis tonnage duty, all toieiga vessels are to pay 2s dollars for health visit, and 23 for certificate, on arriving at Buenos Ay res.
